name: json-parser (udp/json-parser)
baseline: nlohmann/json v2.0.3 (same suite also: json-c 0.12.1, Jansson v2.7, JsonCpp 1.0.0)
workload: nativejson-benchmark: parse in-memory canada.json (2199KB), citm_catalog.json (1737KB) and twitter.json (632KB) into a DOM, plus stringify and prettify of that DOM, using udp/json-parser 1.1.0 together with udp/json-builder for output.
claimed_speedup: Parse time, sum of the three files (derived from page data): udp/json-parser 47.338 ms (29.536 + 13.058 + 4.744) vs Nlohmann 72.476 ms (55.591 + 9.875 + 7.010), about 1.5x faster; vs json-c 134.551 ms about 2.8x, vs Jansson 112.056 ms about 2.4x, vs JsonCpp 165.522 ms about 3.5x (all derived from page data). Stringify sum: 44.512 ms vs Nlohmann 87.732 ms, about 2.0x (derived from page data). Prettify sum: 47.636 ms vs Nlohmann 130.560 ms, about 2.7x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: clang 7.0, 64-bit macOS. Flags are not recorded in the results file; the public build/premake5.lua sets the release configuration to optimize Full with NDEBUG, and gmake builds add -march=native -Wall -Wextra
tradeoffs: Parse memory is higher than nlohmann: 17,195,056 bytes after parsing the three files vs 9,897,872 for Nlohmann (about 1.7x more, derived from page data), though lower than json-c (49,886,288). The README itself claims only a very low footprint, never recursing and never allocating more than needed. C89-portable, no dependencies, small API; the json-builder companion is needed for output.
caveats: Third-party suite by the RapidJSON author (disclosed in its README), but sample numbers are from 2016 with udp/json-parser 1.1.0 and nlohmann/json v2.0.3, both since changed; the repo has seen new commits through 2026-09. The win is not uniform: on citm_catalog.json nlohmann parsed faster (9.875 ms vs 13.058 ms). Conformance rows in the same suite are weak: 26 of 34 parse-validation tests, 37 of 66 double-parse tests and 22 of 27 roundtrip tests pass, so part of the speed may come from looser number and validity handling, while Nlohmann passes 34/34, 66/66 and 23/27. The benchmark wrapper's own comment says stringify is 'Very slow in the current version' although the table row is still faster than nlohmann. The project README itself gives no performance numbers. Flags come from the repo's premake file, not from the result file.

name: json-c
baseline: Jansson v2.7 (same suite also: nlohmann/json v2.0.3, JsonCpp 1.0.0, cJSON 1.5.0)
workload: nativejson-benchmark: serialize the parsed DOM of canada.json (2199KB), citm_catalog.json (1737KB) and twitter.json (632KB) with json_object_to_json_string_ext (plain and pretty modes), json-c 0.12.1.
claimed_speedup: Stringify time, sum of the three files (derived from page data): json-c 30.804 ms (16.260 + 9.990 + 4.554) vs Jansson 69.910 ms (about 2.3x), cJSON 71.283 ms (about 2.3x), Nlohmann 87.732 ms (about 2.9x) and JsonCpp 94.261 ms (about 3.1x). Prettify sum: 49.256 ms vs Jansson 80.380 ms (about 1.6x) and Nlohmann 130.560 ms (about 2.7x), all derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: clang 7.0, 64-bit macOS. Flags are not recorded in the results file; the public build/premake5.lua sets the release configuration to optimize Full with NDEBUG, and gmake builds add -march=native -Wall -Wextra
tradeoffs: Serialization is fast but parsing and memory are not: parse of the three files takes 134.551 ms vs Nlohmann 72.476 ms and udp/json-parser 47.338 ms (sums derived from page data), and the parsed DOM uses 49,886,288 bytes vs 9,897,872 for Nlohmann. Reference-counted object model with C API; the README makes no speed claim and says only that it aims at RFC conformance.
caveats: The only speed win is output (stringify and prettify); parse time is slower than most libraries in the suite and only beats JsonCpp (165.522 ms) and PicoJSON (140.256 ms) by small margins. Third-party suite by the RapidJSON author (disclosed), numbers from 2016 with json-c 0.12.1, which is many releases behind the current repo. Conformance in the same suite: 22 of 34 parse-validation, 57 of 66 double-parse, 9 of 9 string and 27 of 27 roundtrip tests. json-c's README makes no benchmark claim. Flags come from the repo's premake file, not from the result file. Output formatting differs between libraries (for example double formatting), so serialized bytes are not identical across rows.

name: nlohmann/json (JSON for Modern C++)
baseline: JsonCpp 1.0.0 (same suite also: json-c 0.12.1, Jansson v2.7, PicoJSON 1.3.0)
workload: nativejson-benchmark: parse in-memory canada.json (2199KB), citm_catalog.json (1737KB) and twitter.json (632KB) into a DOM with nlohmann/json v2.0.3.
claimed_speedup: Parse time, sum of the three files (derived from page data): Nlohmann 72.476 ms (55.591 + 9.875 + 7.010) vs JsonCpp 165.522 ms (about 2.3x faster), PicoJSON 140.256 ms (about 1.9x), json-c 134.551 ms (about 1.9x) and Jansson 112.056 ms (about 1.6x). Parse memory sum 9,897,872 bytes vs JsonCpp 24,560,400, Jansson 18,319,600 and json-c 49,886,288 (derived from page data). Stringify sum 87.732 ms is only on par with JsonCpp 94.261 ms.
compiler_and_flags: clang 7.0, 64-bit macOS. Flags are not recorded in the results file; the public build/premake5.lua sets the release configuration to optimize Full with NDEBUG, and gmake builds add -march=native -Wall -Wextra
tradeoffs: Chosen for ease of use and single-header integration, not speed. The README's Speed paragraph says: 'There are certainly faster JSON libraries out there' and links the nativejson-benchmark parsing-time chart. Memory per value is small (one pointer plus one byte of type), and in this suite its parse memory is lower than JsonCpp, Jansson and json-c.
caveats: Weak record: the project does not claim to be fast and says faster libraries exist. In the same sample it is mid-pack: RapidJSON parses the three files in 7.932 ms (about 9x faster), cJSON 24.671 ms, udp/json-parser 47.338 ms (all derived from page data), and its prettify sum (130.560 ms) is slower than json-c (49.256 ms), cJSON (71.418 ms) and Jansson (80.380 ms). Numbers are from 2016 with v2.0.3, long before the 3.x series. Newer third-party results put it last: stephenberry/json_performance (June 2025, MacBook Pro M1, Clang 17) lists nlohmann at 15.44 s roundtrip, 86 MB/s write, 81 MB/s read, the slowest of nine libraries, so no current speed advantage is documented. Third-party suite by the RapidJSON author (disclosed). Flags come from the repo's premake file, not the result file.

name: json_struct
workload: stephenberry/json_performance: 1,000,000 iterations of writing and reading one minified test object (nested objects, int/float/double arrays, strings with an escaped string) to and from C++ structs, single core; nlohmann uses hand-written to_json/from_json.
claimed_speedup: Roundtrip time 5.87 s (json_struct) vs 15.44 s (nlohmann), about 2.6x faster (derived from page data); write 178 MB/s vs 86 MB/s, about 2.1x (derived from page data); read 316 MB/s vs 81 MB/s, about 3.9x (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Clang 17 per the README (Apple vs LLVM build not stated); no optimization flags stated. CMakeLists.txt sets only C++20 plus -Wall -Wextra, and src/main.cpp picks the 1,000,000-iteration count under NDEBUG, so a release build is implied. json_struct is fetched from its master branch, nlohmann from release v3.11.3.
tradeoffs: Single header (C++11), maps JSON to structs through JS_OBJ macros, relaxed-parsing options. The same table puts json_struct well behind Glaze (1.01 s), yyjson (1.22 s), reflect_cpp (3.15 s), daw_json_link (3.29 s) and RapidJSON (3.76 s), and about level with Boost.JSON (5.38 s roundtrip, 198 MB/s write, 308 MB/s read).
caveats: Comparison is struct binding, not DOM parsing, and the harness author is the Glaze maintainer (a competitor, but not of json_struct or nlohmann). Optimization flags are not stated and the Clang build (Apple or LLVM) is unspecified; hence tier B, not A. json_struct's own repo has a performance/benchmark.cpp (json_struct vs RapidJSON, simdjson and nlohmann under Catch2) but publishes no results, and the current README makes no performance claim, so the list's 'High performance' wording is not backed by the project itself. json_struct is pulled from master at build time, so the version measured is unknown. COPYING text is an HPND-sell-variant style permissive licence (GitHub shows 'COPYING'; the awesome-cpp tag says MIT).
